title: Extreme outflow velocities and weak UV emission lines indicate quasars shedding their dust cocoons
comment: 30 pages, 27 figures, accepted for publication in A&A
summary: The recently discovered low-ionisation broad absorption line (LoBAL) quasar GQ 1309$+$2904 is unusual due to its very broad, highly blueshifted absorption troughs and an absence of broad emission lines except for ${\mathrm{H} α}$. In this paper, we present observations of six quasars that appear very similar to GQ 1309$+$2904 in the rest-frame ultraviolet (UV). We measure the systemic redshifts of these quasars to be $z\approx$ 2.07--3.28 from detected ${\mathrm{H} α}$ emission lines. We confirm that all targets are quasars with highly blueshifted BALs possessing high-speed outflows with velocities up to $\sim 0.16\,c$, and five of them are confidently identified as LoBAL quasars. Based on ${\mathrm{H} α}$ emission, black hole masses and Eddington ratios of these quasars are $M_{\mathrm{BH}} \approx 10^{8.7}$--$10^{9.4}\,M_{\odot}$ and $L_{\mathrm{bol}} / L_{\mathrm{Edd}} \approx$ 0.14--0.34, indicating that their central black holes are very massive and active. Every quasar in our sample exhibits a very flat or reddened continuum. The spectral shapes of three objects are well-fitted by a normal quasar composite reddened by a Small-Magellanic-Cloud-like (SMC-like) extinction curve, while the other three require a steeper extinction law. Broad-band ($BVR$) polarimetry for two of the latter group (plus GQ 1309$+$2904) reveals their low polarisations, consistent with low inclination (more face-on) angles. We propose that these objects are weak emission-line quasars (WLQs) observed through the disc wind, caught emerging from their dust cocoons. As quasars shed their cocoons, dust grains in the disc wind are shattered into smaller particles, producing the UV-steeper extinction curve observed along the outflow. We present a schematic illustration of this shedding process that can account for the peculiar spectral features observed in our sample.

AI.tldr: This paper identifies and analyzes six quasars similar to GQ 1309+2904 — LoBAL quasars with highly blueshifted absorption troughs, fast outflows (up to 0.16c), massive black holes (10^8.7–10^9.4 M⊙), Eddington ratios 0.14–0.34, and reddened continua. Some exhibit SMC-like extinction, others require a steeper UV extinction law. Low polarimetry suggests face-on orientation. The authors propose these are weak emission-line quasars (WLQs) seen through disc winds emerging from dust cocoons, with dust shattering causing the steeper extinction.
AI.motivation: To understand the nature of the unusual LoBAL quasar GQ 1309+2904 by finding and analyzing similar objects, thereby explaining their peculiar spectral features including very broad blueshifted BALs, absence of broad emission lines except Hα, and reddened continua.
AI.method: Observations of six UV-selected quasars similar to GQ 1309+2904; systemic redshift measurement from Hα emission; black hole mass and Eddington ratio estimation; continuum fitting with SMC-like and steeper extinction laws; broad-band BVR polarimetry for two objects plus GQ 1309+2904.
AI.result: All six are quasars with highly blueshifted BALs and outflows up to ~0.16c; five are LoBALs. BH masses ~10^8.7–10^9.4 M⊙; Eddington ratios 0.14–0.34. Continuum is flat/reddened: three fit SMC-like extinction, three require a steeper law. Low polarisation indicates low inclination (face-on).
AI.conclusion: These objects are likely WLQs observed through disc winds emerging from dust cocoons. Dust grain shattering in the outflow produces the steeper UV extinction. A schematic shedding process is proposed to explain the observed spectral features.

title: The fingerprint of primordial mass segregation on the tidal tails of star clusters
summary: We investigate the effect of primordial mass segregation (PMS) in shaping the tidal tail structures of star clusters, searching for any trace of PMS on the tails at both early and late evolutionary stages. Through N-body simulations, we analyze clusters with two different degrees of PMS at various Galactocentric distances (R_G), considering two black hole retention scenarios. Our findings reveal that PMS influences early cluster expansion and the formation of tidal tails with a bottom-heavy stellar mass function, this being more pronounced at smaller R_G but diminishes over time. Primordially segregated clusters exhibit denser, unified, and longer tail structures compared to non-segregated clusters. The mean stellar mass distribution along the tails shows distinct patterns for primordially segregated and non-segregated clusters, converging at later evolutionary stages. The retention of stellar remnants has a weak impact on the mean mass distribution along the tails and on its morphology. We find that although mean mass differences persist along the tidal tails, the rate of change in primordially mass-segregated clusters eventually converges with that of non-segregated clusters, suggesting that the influence of primordial mass segregation on the tidal tails gradually diminishes over the course of cluster evolution.

AI.tldr: This study uses N-body simulations to examine how primordial mass segregation (PMS) affects tidal tail structures of star clusters. PMS causes denser, longer tails with bottom-heavy stellar mass functions early on, especially at smaller Galactocentric distances, but these effects diminish over time as segregated and non-segregated clusters converge in their evolutionary behavior.
AI.motivation: To investigate whether primordial mass segregation leaves observable traces on tidal tail structures of star clusters across different evolutionary stages, and to understand how this influences tail morphology and stellar mass distribution.
AI.method: N-body simulations of star clusters with two degrees of PMS at various Galactocentric distances, considering two black hole retention scenarios.
AI.result: PMS causes denser, longer, more unified tidal tails with bottom-heavy mass functions, especially at smaller R_G. Mean mass distributions differ between segregated and non-segregated clusters but converge at later stages. Black hole retention has weak effects on tail morphology and mass distribution.
AI.conclusion: The influence of primordial mass segregation on tidal tails gradually diminishes over cluster evolution, with segregated and non-segregated clusters converging in their tail properties at later stages.

title: IRIS: Deciphering Spectral-Line Imagery of the Galactic Center by Machine-Learning on Simulations
summary:
In understanding the 3D structure of the Milky Way's Central Molecular Zone (CMZ), we are limited by our edge-on perspective. Towards addressing this problem, we introduce Imagery Reversion Informed by Simulation (IRIS). IRIS is a novel machine-learning code base featuring a deep convolutional neural network (CNN), which we have designed to translate edge-on observations of our Milky Way Galaxy into top-down images by training on data generated from AREPO galaxy simulations and synthetic observations of those simulations.
  We develop a large custom dataset on which we train our bespoke model, and then test the trained model on synthetic data to probe the potential of this machine-learning method, which we call supervised reversion. We then apply our trained model to real observations from the SEDIGISM 13CO(2-1) survey, yielding new top-down views of our CMZ. Though our SEDIGISM reversions are not fully consistent across model training runs, we posit that this lack of convergence can be alleviated by expansion of the training dataset. We argue that these results represent a strong proof-of-concept for the use of supervised reversion to decipher our CMZ's 3D structure.
  Crucial in generating our training dataset's 100k synthetic observations, we introduce IRIS Synthetic Observation (IRIS-SO), a new GPU-accelerated and fully differentiable code implemented in PyTorch for the non-LTE synthetic observation of spectral lines and dust. We find that IRIS-SO provides up to 10,000x speedups in comparison to the synthetic-observation code RADMC-3D. We release all the IRIS code open-source at https://github.com/bldubois/IRIS.

AI.tldr: IRIS is a machine-learning framework using a deep CNN trained on AREPO galaxy simulations to convert edge-on Milky Way CMZ observations into top-down views. It includes a GPU-accelerated synthetic observation code (IRIS-SO) that achieves up to 10,000x speedup over RADMC-3D. Results on SEDIGISM data show proof-of-concept for supervised reversion of 3D CMZ structure.
AI.motivation: Our edge-on perspective limits understanding of the 3D structure of the Milky Way's Central Molecular Zone (CMZ).
AI.method: A deep convolutional neural network (CNN) is trained on synthetic data from AREPO galaxy simulations with synthetic observations. The trained model is applied to real SEDIGISM 13CO(2-1) survey data. A new GPU-accelerated synthetic observation code, IRIS-SO, generates 100k training examples.
AI.result: Supervised reversion yields top-down views of the CMZ from SEDIGISM data, though results are not fully consistent across training runs. IRIS-SO achieves up to 10,000x speedup over RADMC-3D.
AI.conclusion: The results demonstrate a strong proof-of-concept for using supervised reversion to decipher the CMZ's 3D structure. Lack of convergence can be alleviated by expanding the training dataset.

title: Fractional-Dimension Gravity and the Milky Way Galaxy
comment: 19 pages, including 6 figures. Eight paper on Fractional-Dimension Gravity
summary:
In this work, we focus our analysis of Fractional-Dimension Gravity (FDG) on our home galaxy, the Milky Way (MW), by using the latest Gaia DR3 data as well as previous rotation curve (RC) data for this galaxy. FDG is an alternative gravitational model (previously known as Newtonian Fractional-Dimension Gravity - NFDG) which does not require the dark matter (DM) paradigm.
  The MW is studied here with the methods of FDG and its observed rotation curves are successfully reproduced by using a variable fractional dimension $D\left (R\right)$, following previous studies of several other galaxies which were analyzed with the same methodology. An alternative dimension function $D_{m}\left(R \right)$, based on the mass-dimension field equation, was also used and yielded less accurate fits to the experimental data.
  In addition, we also considered possible implications of the FDG metric, based on the presence of additional weights, on the structure of Special Relativity (SR) for spacetimes with fractional dimension. One notable outcome of this analysis is the possibility of an effective superluminal motion in galactic regions where the space dimension is $D<3$. Although this result is very speculative, it opens interesting new perspectives for possible interstellar travel in our galaxy.

AI.tldr: This paper applies Fractional-Dimension Gravity (FDG) to the Milky Way using Gaia DR3 data, successfully reproducing observed rotation curves without dark matter, and explores speculative implications for superluminal motion in regions with fractional dimension D<3.
AI.motivation: To test Fractional-Dimension Gravity (FDG) as an alternative to the dark matter paradigm by analyzing the Milky Way's rotation curves using the latest Gaia DR3 data, and to explore potential implications of the FDG metric for special relativity and interstellar travel.
AI.method: Applied FDG (formerly NFDG) to Milky Way rotation curve data from Gaia DR3 and previous datasets, using a variable fractional dimension D(R) and an alternative dimension function D_m(R) based on the mass-dimension field equation.
AI.result: Observed Milky Way rotation curves were successfully reproduced using variable D(R); the alternative D_m(R) function yielded less accurate fits. The analysis also suggested possible effective superluminal motion in galactic regions where D<3.
AI.conclusion: FDG can explain Milky Way rotation curves without dark matter, and the speculative possibility of superluminal motion in low-dimensional regions opens new perspectives for interstellar travel, though further investigation is needed.

title: Pulsar Science with the SKAO
comment: 13 pages, 2 figures, Published in Advancing Astrophysics with the SKA II (AASKAII), 2026 (arXiv:2606.20366). Report number AASKAII/Joshi01. Advancing Astrophysics with the SKA II (AASKA II) outlines the transformative scientific advances that will be enabled by the SKA telescopes. An earlier version of this chapter was published in The Open Journal of Astrophysics with arXiv ID: arXiv:2512.16152
summary: The large instantaneous sensitivity, wide frequency coverage and flexible observation modes, with large number of beams in the sky, are the main features of the SKA observatory's two telescopes, the SKA-Low and the SKA-Mid. Owing to these capabilities, the SKAO telescopes are going to be a game-changer for radio astronomy in general and pulsar astronomy in particular. Eleven chapters in this book describe their impact on different areas of pulsar science. In this overview article each chapter is briefly summarised and the inter-relationship between different pulsar science use cases are explored: new deep surveys, covering the Galactic field, globular clusters and the Galactic centre, will discover thousands of new pulsars; these will form the backbone for studies of neutron star physics and of their environments. The enhanced understanding provided by these studies will feed into the main contributions to fundamental physics from pulsar astronomy: testing relativistic gravity, studying gravitational waves in the nano-Hz regime and studying the equation of state of nuclear matter. Synergies with other science cases are also highlighted throughout this overview.

AI.tldr: This overview article summarizes 11 chapters on how SKA-Low and SKA-Mid telescopes will revolutionize pulsar astronomy through deep surveys, neutron star physics, and fundamental physics tests (gravity, gravitational waves, nuclear equation of state).
AI.motivation: To highlight how the SKA observatory's telescopes (SKA-Low and SKA-Mid) will transform pulsar astronomy due to their large sensitivity, wide frequency coverage, flexible observation modes, and large number of beams.
AI.method: The paper provides an overview by summarizing 11 chapters covering different areas of pulsar science, exploring inter-relationships between pulsar science use cases, and highlighting synergies with other science cases.
AI.result: New deep surveys (Galactic field, globular clusters, Galactic centre) will discover thousands of new pulsars, forming the backbone for studies of neutron star physics and environments, which in turn feed into fundamental physics contributions.
AI.conclusion: The SKAO telescopes will be a game-changer for radio astronomy and pulsar science, enabling advances in relativistic gravity tests, nano-Hz gravitational wave studies, and nuclear matter equation of state research.

title: Radiative filtering unifies broad-line phenomenology in active galactic nuclei
comment: 12 pages, 5 figures, as Letter to Astrophysical Journal
summary: Broad emission lines (BELs) are a defining feature of active galactic nuclei (AGNs), yet they weaken or disappear in both very low- and very high-accretion systems. These regimes are typically treated separately, and a unified physical explanation has remained elusive. Here we show that this behavior arises if line formation is governed not by the intrinsic luminosity of the central engine, but by the ionizing radiation field that survives filtering before reaching the broad-line region (BLR). In this picture, line production depends on the product of intrinsic ionizing capability and an effective transmission. Because the former increases from low accretion rates while the latter declines at high accretion rates, the effective ionizing field naturally develops a finite and non-universal window for BEL formation. This framework unifies the absence or extreme faintness of BELs in low-luminosity AGNs, LINERs, and weak-line quasars (WLQs), and accounts for the Baldwin effect and the $R_{\rm Fe}$ trend. It also necessarily implies the breakdown of standard BLR-based scaling relations in extreme accretion regimes. We show that a minimal quantitative realization reproduces this behavior across black-hole mass, accretion rate, and radiative efficiency. These results suggest that AGN emission-line phenomenology is governed by global regulation of the ionizing radiation field rather than by mere presence or condition of local gas.

AI.tldr: Broad emission lines in AGNs weaken or disappear at both very low and very high accretion rates because their formation depends on the filtered ionizing radiation field surviving to the broad-line region, rather than on intrinsic luminosity, creating a finite and non-universal window for BEL production.
AI.motivation: Broad emission lines (BELs) weaken or disappear in both very low- and very high-accretion AGN systems, which are typically treated as separate regimes with no unified physical explanation.
AI.method: The authors propose that BEL formation depends on the product of intrinsic ionizing capability and effective transmission through filtering, rather than intrinsic luminosity alone, and present a minimal quantitative realization across black-hole mass, accretion rate, and radiative efficiency.
AI.result: The effective ionizing field develops a finite, non-universal window for BEL formation, naturally explaining the absence/faintness of BELs in low-luminosity AGNs, LINERs, and WLQs, as well as the Baldwin effect and R_Fe trend.
AI.conclusion: AGN emission-line phenomenology is governed by global regulation of the ionizing radiation field rather than by the mere presence or condition of local gas, implying the breakdown of standard BLR-based scaling relations in extreme accretion regimes.

title: A possible high-redshift origin for the short GRB 061201: implications of a compact binary merger beyond cosmic noon
comment: 8 pages, 4 figures, submitted
summary: Short gamma-ray bursts (GRBs) at redshift z>2 remain exceptionally rare, yet they are crucial for tracing compact binary mergers in the early Universe and understanding their role in the production of r-process elements. GRB 061201 is an unusual and still debated event: although its optical afterglow was accurately localized, no secure coincident host galaxy was identified, and the proposed associations with nearby galaxies all require a large separation between the GRB and its birth site. In this work, we revisit GRB 061201 and argue that the observations are more naturally explained if the burst occurred within a faint F322W2~28.4 AB mag galaxy at z>2. By combining constraints from the afterglow and deep near-infrared imaging from JWST, we show that a distant origin provides a coherent explanation of the burst phenomenology. If confirmed, GRB 061201 would represent one of the most distant short GRBs known, extending the observed compact merger population to an epoch when the Universe was only about two billion years old.

AI.tldr: GRB 061201, an unusual short gamma-ray burst with no clear host galaxy association, is reanalyzed and argued to originate from a faint galaxy at z>2, which would make it one of the most distant short GRBs known, suggesting compact binary mergers occurred when the Universe was ~2 billion years old.
AI.motivation: Short GRBs at z>2 are extremely rare but essential for tracing compact binary mergers in the early Universe and their role in r-process element production. GRB 061201 has been debated due to the lack of a secure host galaxy association.
AI.method: The authors revisit GRB 061201 by combining afterglow constraints with deep near-infrared JWST imaging to evaluate whether the burst originated from a faint F322W2~28.4 AB mag galaxy at z>2.
AI.result: A distant origin at z>2 provides a coherent explanation for the burst phenomenology, resolving the previously puzzling lack of a coincident host galaxy.
AI.conclusion: If confirmed, GRB 061201 would be one of the most distant short GRBs known, extending the observed compact merger population to when the Universe was ~2 billion years old.

title: The Galactic Centre G+0.633-0.0604 molecular cloud: a new astrochemical gold mine. I. Gas physical properties
comment: 20 pages, 11 figures, 8 tables, 6 appendix - Accepted for publication in Astronomy & Astrophysics
summary: In the Central Molecular Zone (CMZ), shocks play a key role in triggering star formation and driving chemical enrichment. The Sgr B2 complex is a prime template, hosting massive protoclusters (N, M, S) and the northern G+0.693 cloud, which exhibits shock-induced prestellar signatures. We report on G+0.633-0.0604, a newly identified shock-dominated and chemically rich cloud at the southern edge of Sgr B2, where the next star formation episodes are proposed. We characterise its physical properties and the shocks shaping it. We present analyses on CH$_3$CCH, CH$_3$CN, HC$_3$N, HNCO and several isotopologues of CO to infer the gas $T_{\rm kin}$ and density, using high-sensitivity spectral surveys from the Yebes 40m, IRAM 30m and APEX radio telescopes that covered ~100 GHz across the 31-275 GHz range. We also used 3 mm IRAM 30m mosaics (13'$\times$13') of Sgr B2 in HC$_3$N, HNCO and C$_2$H$_5$OH to probe G+0.633 environment. We identify three velocity components: a narrow main one (C1, $v_{\rm LSR}$~48.5 km/s; FWHM~10 km/s), and two broader, fainter components at higher velocities, C2 (~61 km/s; ~13 km/s) and C3 (~89 km/s; ~18 km/s), all showing similar properties ($T_{\rm kin}$~55-90 K, $N_{\rm H_2}$~(3-7)$\times$10$^{22}$ cm$^{-2}$, $n_{\rm H_2}$~(0.5-2.5)$\times$10$^{4}$ cm$^{-3}$) and extended distributions. C1 delineates G+0.633 physically and coincides with a peak in HNCO, supporting a shock-driven origin likely rooted in the cloud-cloud collision shaping Sgr B2 and also traced by C2, which extends north to G+0.693. C3 is kinematically unlinked and related to large-scale CMZ dynamics. Of the three, C1 may represent a very early protocluster phase, yet to be confirmed. G+0.633 thus emerges as a new shock-dominated CMZ cloud resembling G+0.693, providing another unique laboratory to investigate how shocks drive molecular complexity and regulate the onset of cluster formation in the CMZ.

AI.tldr: G+0.633-0.0604 is a newly identified shock-dominated, chemically rich molecular cloud at the southern edge of Sgr B2 in the Central Molecular Zone. Multi-telescope spectral surveys reveal three velocity components (C1, C2, C3) with similar physical properties (T_kin ~55-90 K, N_H2 ~(3-7)×10^22 cm^-2, n_H2 ~(0.5-2.5)×10^4 cm^-3). C1 delimits the cloud and shows shock signatures (HNCO peak), likely from cloud-cloud collision; C2 extends to G+0.693; C3 is kinematically unrelated. G+0.633 may be a very early protocluster phase, offering a new laboratory to study shock-driven chemistry and cluster formation in the CMZ.
AI.motivation: To identify and characterize a new shock-dominated, chemically rich molecular cloud (G+0.633-0.0604) at the southern edge of Sgr B2, where the next star formation episodes are proposed, and to understand how shocks drive molecular complexity and regulate the onset of cluster formation in the Central Molecular Zone.
AI.method: High-sensitivity spectral surveys from Yebes 40m, IRAM 30m, and APEX radio telescopes covering ~100 GHz across 31-275 GHz, plus 3 mm IRAM 30m mosaics (13'×13') of Sgr B2. Analysis of CH3CCH, CH3CN, HC3N, HNCO, and CO isotopologues to infer gas kinetic temperature and density.
AI.result: Three velocity components identified: C1 (v_LSR ~48.5 km/s, FWHM ~10 km/s), C2 (~61 km/s, ~13 km/s), C3 (~89 km/s, ~18 km/s). All share similar T_kin (~55-90 K), N_H2 (~(3-7)×10^22 cm^-2), n_H2 (~(0.5-2.5)×10^4 cm^-3), and extended distributions. C1 coincides with a HNCO peak supporting shock origin; C2 extends north to G+0.693; C3 is kinematically unrelated. C1 may represent a very early protocluster phase.
AI.conclusion: G+0.633-0.0604 emerges as a new shock-dominated CMZ cloud resembling G+0.693, providing another unique laboratory to investigate shock-driven molecular complexity and the onset of cluster formation in the Central Molecular Zone.

title: X-ray polarization in magnetized neutron stars
comment: 18 pages, 8 figures
summary: X-ray polarimetry has opened a new window into understanding the physics around magnetized compact objects. IXPE detection of linear polarization from such systems has prompted a new spurt of theoretical modeling. Our study is based on the dominant paradigm that the observed polarization arises from the scattering of photons around highly magnetized systems. Our main focus is the dependence of the polarization of the scattered light on properties of the incoming light, i.e., geometry and the polarization state, and the determination of the spectral shape of the polarized light for a wide range of magnetic field strengths. We also analyze the impact of vacuum birefringence on photon polarization. We show that, generically, we expect a higher linear degree of polarization from magnetars as compared to normal pulsars, which is in agreement with IXPE observations. Under some conditions, our study helps to understand the observed degree of polarization from normal pulsars and low-magnetized neutron stars and their spectral dependence. However, we cannot conclusively explain the spectral shape of the observed polarization for magnetars using only a single component emission from scattering in a strong magnetic field. This probably points to the system being more complex, e.g., multi-component, than our study allows for. Upcoming X-ray polarimeters with broader energy coverage could probe some of our other predictions, e.g., the spectral shape of the polarized light close to the resonance frequency.

AI.tldr: The paper studies X-ray polarization from magnetized compact objects, showing that scattering in strong magnetic fields predicts higher linear polarization from magnetars than normal pulsars (consistent with IXPE data), but cannot fully explain magnetar polarization spectra with a single-component model, suggesting more complex emission processes.
AI.motivation: To understand the physics around magnetized compact objects using X-ray polarimetry, motivated by IXPE detections of linear polarization from such systems.
AI.method: Theoretical modeling of polarization arising from photon scattering in highly magnetized systems, analyzing dependence on incoming light properties (geometry, polarization state) and magnetic field strength, including vacuum birefringence effects.
AI.result: Higher linear polarization degree predicted for magnetars compared to normal pulsars (matching IXPE); spectral dependence of polarized light explained for normal pulsars and low-magnetized neutron stars under some conditions, but not for magnetars with a single-component scattering model.
AI.conclusion: Magnetar polarization likely requires multi-component emission models; upcoming broad-energy X-ray polarimeters could test predictions near the resonance frequency.

title: Post-starburst Galaxies with Active Galactic Nucleus: Properties and Evolutionary Sequences
comment: 25 pages, 12 figures. Accepted for publication in The Astrophysical Journal
summary: Post-starburst (PSB) galaxies, identified by strong Balmer absorption and weak nebular emission, provide a key laboratory for studying rapid quenching. Using the final data release of the SDSS-IV MaNGA survey, we follow the traditional PSB selection criteria of Chen et al. (2019) and develop a new method to identify regions that simultaneously exhibit PSB features and nuclear activities (AGN-PSBs). Our final sample comprises 48 AGN-PSBs, 92 central PSBs (CPSBs), 89 ring-like PSBs (RPSBs), and 828 irregular PSBs (IPSBs). We find the global and spatially resolved properties of CPSBs and RPSBs are consistent with the results of Chen et al. (2019). In this work, we focus on the properties of AGN-PSBs, comparing them with CPSBs, RPSBs, and control galaxies. Similar to CPSBs and RPSBs, AGN-PSBs show positive $\mathrm{D}_{n}4000$ gradients relative to negative $\mathrm{D}_{n}4000$ gradients of their controls, which indicates younger stellar populations in the central region than that in the outskirt. Among the three sub-types, high-mass CPSBs (H-CPSBs, with $\log(M_{*}/M_{\odot})>9.5$) display the highest incidence of merger remnants and gas--star kinematic misalignment, consistent with a merger/interaction-dominated origin. AGN-PSBs and RPSBs, however, show lower and comparable fractions of merger remnants and gas--star kinematic misalignment, favoring less violent external mechanisms. Based on radial profiles of mass-weighted age and $V_{\rm star}/σ_{\rm star}$, we suggest that RPSBs can evolve into AGN-PSBs, whereas H-CPSBs likely follow a distinct evolutionary pathway. The existence of RPSBs and IPSBs also indicates that AGN feedback is not a necessary condition for the formation of PSB.

AI.tldr: This paper studies post-starburst (PSB) galaxies using SDSS-IV MaNGA data, classifying them into AGN-PSBs, central PSBs (CPSBs), ring-like PSBs (RPSBs), and irregular PSBs (IPSBs). AGN-PSBs show positive Dn4000 gradients like other PSBs. High-mass CPSBs show merger features, while AGN-PSBs and RPSBs show less violent origins. RPSBs may evolve into AGN-PSBs, and AGN feedback is not necessary for PSB formation.
AI.motivation: To understand rapid quenching mechanisms in galaxies by studying post-starburst (PSB) galaxies, particularly investigating the connection between PSB features and nuclear activity, and exploring different evolutionary pathways among PSB subtypes.
AI.method: Using SDSS-IV MaNGA final data release, following traditional PSB selection criteria (Chen et al. 2019) and developing a new method to identify AGN-PSB regions. Classified 48 AGN-PSBs, 92 CPSBs, 89 RPSBs, and 828 IPSBs. Analyzed global and spatially resolved properties, including Dn4000 gradients, merger fractions, kinematic misalignment, and radial profiles of mass-weighted age and V_star/σ_star.
AI.result: AGN-PSBs show positive Dn4000 gradients (younger centers). High-mass CPSBs have highest merger remnants and kinematic misalignment. AGN-PSBs and RPSBs have lower merger fractions. RPSBs may evolve into AGN-PSBs; H-CPSBs follow a distinct pathway. AGN feedback is not necessary for PSB formation.
AI.conclusion: Different PSB subtypes likely have distinct formation pathways: mergers drive high-mass CPSBs, while less violent mechanisms drive AGN-PSBs and RPSBs. RPSBs may represent a precursor phase to AGN-PSBs. The existence of RPSBs and IPSBs suggests AGN feedback is not essential for PSB formation.

title: Constraining the near-source relativistic wind medium using Fast Radio Burst circular polarization data
comment: Comments encouraged. 21 pages, 10 figures, 1 table. Submitted for review
summary: Fast Radio Bursts (FRBs) exhibit diverse spectro-temporal characteristics, which can probe vital propagation and source physics via Stokes polarimetry. We investigate whether the circular polarization (Stokes $V$) observed in some bursts is produced by Faraday conversion in the near-source wind of magnetars rather than being intrinsic to the source. Our calculation includes the increase in the effective mass of $e^\pm$ in the presence of the FRB wave. We find that Faraday conversion in the magnetar wind can explain the broad range of observed circular polarization in FRBs, including its frequent non-detection. Observationally derived upper limits on $V$ provide stringent constraints on the wind luminosity, magnetization, bulk Lorentz factor, and effective particle mass when ions are present. When available, frequency resolved Stokes spectra offer direct estimates of the wind environment. The Stokes parameters can undergo rapid oscillations with frequency in the high-wind/low-FRB-luminosity regime, resulting in Stokes-V depolarization. Bursts with significantly lower luminosities than typical FRBs can also develop measurable circular polarization, within the model framework. Additionally, separate zones are favored for significant circular polarization and rotation measure, when the model is applicable. The model constrains instantaneous wind parameters for several sources, including FRB 20201124A, FRB 20180301A, and SGR 1935+2154. This work represents the first instance in which properties of winds from compact objects associated with FRBs are inferred from polarization data.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates whether the circular polarization (Stokes V) observed in some Fast Radio Bursts (FRBs) is produced by Faraday conversion in the near-source wind of magnetars, rather than being intrinsic to the source. The authors find that this mechanism can explain the broad range of observed circular polarization, and use polarization data to infer wind properties of several FRB sources.
AI.motivation: To determine whether circular polarization in FRBs arises from Faraday conversion in magnetar winds or is intrinsic to the source, and to use polarization observations to probe the near-source wind environment.
AI.method: The authors model Faraday conversion in magnetar winds, including the increase in effective mass of e± pairs in the presence of the FRB wave, and compare predictions with observed Stokes V data from multiple FRB sources.
AI.result: Faraday conversion in magnetar winds can explain the observed range of circular polarization in FRBs. Upper limits on V constrain wind luminosity, magnetization, Lorentz factor, and effective particle mass. Stokes parameters can oscillate rapidly with frequency in high-wind/low-luminosity regimes, causing depolarization. Lower-luminosity bursts can also develop measurable circular polarization. Separate zones are favored for significant circular polarization and rotation measure.
AI.conclusion: This is the first work that infers properties of winds from compact objects associated with FRBs using polarization data, providing constraints on instantaneous wind parameters for sources including FRB 20201124A, FRB 20180301A, and SGR 1935+2154.

title: Distance Determination of Southern Galactic Plane Supernova Remnants with the Mopra CO Survey and DECaPS 3D Dust Map
comment: 31 pages, 17 figures, accepted for publication in The Astronomical Journal (AJ)
summary: Accurate distance measurements to supernova remnants (SNRs) are crucial for understanding their physical properties, evolutionary processes, and role in the Galactic interstellar medium (ISM) cycle. In this study, we apply for the first time to the southern Galactic plane a distance determination method that utilizes CO emission data from the Mopra survey to identify molecular clouds (MCs) interacting with SNRs. By combining this with extinction-distance profiles from the DECaPS three-dimensional (3D) extinction map, we directly measure the distances to the associated MCs, thereby obtaining precise distances to the remnants. To overcome the extinction-missing bias in extremely dense regions where the 3D map suffers from a deficit of background stars, we supplement our analysis with two-dimensional (2D) extinction maps as cross-validation. Applying this method, we have derived precise distances for nine SNRs: G290.1-0.8 (7.32+0.60/-0.47 kpc), G292.2-0.5 (10.85+0.43/-0.68 kpc), G296.1-0.5 (4.59+0.18/-0.19 kpc), G296.8-0.3 (8.74+0.40/-0.29 kpc), G298.6-0.0 (6.50 +/- 0.21 kpc), G312.4-0.4 (3.60+0.19/-0.23 kpc), G332.4-0.4 (2.66+0.23/-0.15 kpc), G335.2+0.1 (2.76+0.37/-0.31 kpc), and G353.6-0.7 (1.81+0.18/-0.14 kpc). Additionally, we established a robust lower distance limit of 1.34 kpc for G351.7+0.8.

AI.tldr: This study presents a new distance determination method for supernova remnants (SNRs) in the southern Galactic plane, using CO emission data from the Mopra survey to identify interacting molecular clouds and combining it with DECaPS 3D extinction maps, with 2D maps as cross-validation. Precise distances were derived for nine SNRs, and a lower distance limit was established for a tenth.
AI.motivation: Accurate distances to SNRs are essential for understanding their physical properties, evolution, and role in the Galactic ISM cycle, but precise distance measurements remain challenging.
AI.method: A novel distance determination method using CO emission data from the Mopra survey to identify molecular clouds interacting with SNRs, combined with extinction-distance profiles from the DECaPS 3D extinction map. Two-dimensional extinction maps were used as cross-validation to mitigate extinction-missing bias in dense regions.
AI.result: Precise distances for nine SNRs (ranging from 1.81 to 10.85 kpc) and a robust lower distance limit of 1.34 kpc for G351.7+0.8.
AI.conclusion: The method successfully provides precise distances to SNRs in the southern Galactic plane, improving our understanding of these objects and their role in the Galactic environment.

title: AI-enabled gravitational-waves searches for binary neutron stars at optimal sensitivity
summary: Gravitational Waves (GWs) represent the newest window of astronomy, furthering our understanding of compact objects like black holes and neutron stars in the Universe. The signal from two merging neutron stars is especially interesting since it brings the prospect of concordant electromagnetic and neutrino emissions. Such multi-messenger observations have a transformational impact on fundamental physics, nuclear matter, astrophysics, and gravity. It was first witnessed in 2017 with the detection of the binary neutron star (BNS) merger GW170817. However, searching for BNS signals in real-time in the LIGO-Virgo-KAGRA (LVK) GW detectors presents a computational challenge, as the data streaming out must be matched against $\sim$ million reference waveforms, which requires up to a thousand CPU cores. We present a different approach using neural networks to learn the presence of a signal in the data. Our algorithm, called Aframe, was deployed in the LVK's fourth observing run and was the first artificial intelligence (AI)-enabled search to detect multiple binary black holes (BBHs) live. In this work, we demonstrate that the approach extends to the lower-mass BNS regime, and is the first AI-enabled search that achieves sensitivity comparable to matched-filter pipelines at lower computational and latency costs. The challenge of the longer-duration BNS signals is addressed by heterodyning the data, following which the network architecture used for BBHs is sufficient to distinguish signal versus background. We also show that this analysis requires a single non-flagship GPU for online deployment. Furthermore, the design and adoption of inference-as-a-service tools allow rapid offline analysis using a distributed pool of GPU resources. Hence, aside from the use case of rapid online data analysis, we also establish the use of Aframe for efficient archival data analysis.

AI.tldr: Aframe is an AI-enabled gravitational wave search using neural networks, deployed live in LVK's O4 run. It achieves comparable sensitivity to matched-filter pipelines for binary neutron star mergers at lower computational and latency cost, requiring only a single non-flagship GPU for online deployment.
AI.motivation: Real-time searching for binary neutron star (BNS) merger signals in LIGO-Virgo-KAGRA (LVK) GW detectors presents a computational challenge, as streaming data must be matched against ~million reference waveforms, requiring up to a thousand CPU cores.
AI.method: The authors use neural networks to learn the presence of signals in data. For longer-duration BNS signals, they apply heterodyning to the data, then use the same network architecture previously used for binary black holes (BBHs) to distinguish signal versus background. They employ inference-as-a-service tools for distributed GPU resource utilization.
AI.result: Aframe was the first AI-enabled search to detect multiple BBHs live in LVK's O4 run. It extends to the lower-mass BNS regime with sensitivity comparable to matched-filter pipelines at lower computational and latency costs. Requires a single non-flagship GPU for online deployment.
AI.conclusion: Aframe enables efficient online and offline archival data analysis for both BBH and BNS gravitational wave signals, reducing computational requirements significantly compared to traditional matched-filter approaches.

title: Resolved HI and Environmental Dynamics
comment: Published in Advancing Astrophysics with the SKA II (AASKAII), 2026 (arXiv:2606.20366). Report-no: AASKAII/Ramatsoku01. Advancing Astrophysics with the SKA II (AASKAII) outlines the transformative scientific advances that will be enabled by the SKA telescopes
summary: Spatially resolved, deep HI observations from SKA precursors and pathfinders such as MeerKAT, FAST, and ASKAP have demonstrated their ability to reveal the complex interactions between galaxies and their environments. These include, but are not limited to, recent observations of the Virgo cluster showing that the hydrodynamical effects of ram pressure stripping can operate effectively at unexpectedly large cluster-centric distances. In the Fornax cluster, the discovery of long HI tails with mixed tidal-ram-pressure origins indicates the interplay between gravitational and hydrodynamical mechanisms. Similar HI features in nearby filaments and galaxy groups, where ram pressure is expected to be weak, highlight the influence of hydrodynamical processes even in low-density environments. Multi-resolution studies have further revealed signs of cold gas accretion and HI replenishment driven by tidal interactions. While highly informative, these studies remain limited to small, specific regions of the sky. With SKA-mid AA4, it will become possible to carry out deep, spatially resolved HI imaging over hundreds of square degrees, covering environments from isolated galaxies to filaments. By reaching column-density sensitivities between $1.0 \times 10^{18}$ and $\sim 1.0 \times 10^{19}~\mathrm{cm^{-2}}$ at physical resolutions of $\sim$10 and $\sim$1 - 2 kpc, respectively, and by enabling sensitive, contiguous observations of wide areas within short integrations, SKA-mid AA4 will allow the construction of large, statistically representative samples of galaxies and detailed studies of environmental mechanisms operating across the full range of these less-studied environments at resolved scales.

AI.tldr: SKA precursors/pathfinders have revealed gas-galaxy interactions in various environments, but studies remain limited to small sky areas. SKA-mid AA4 will enable deep, spatially resolved HI imaging over hundreds of square degrees, covering diverse environments at high sensitivity and resolution, allowing statistically significant galaxy samples to study environmental mechanisms at resolved scales.
AI.motivation: Current spatially resolved HI observations from SKA precursors (MeerKAT, FAST, ASKAP) are limited to small, specific sky regions, preventing the construction of large, statistically representative samples needed to fully understand environmental mechanisms across the full range of galaxy environments.
AI.method: SKA-mid AA4 will carry out deep, spatially resolved HI imaging over hundreds of square degrees, reaching column-density sensitivities of 1.0×10¹⁸–1.0×10¹⁹ cm⁻² at physical resolutions of ~10 kpc and ~1–2 kpc, with sensitive, contiguous wide-area observations in short integrations.
AI.result: SKA-mid AA4 will enable construction of large, statistically representative galaxy samples and detailed studies of environmental mechanisms (ram pressure stripping, tidal interactions, cold gas accretion) across isolated galaxies, filaments, groups, and clusters at resolved scales.
AI.conclusion: SKA-mid AA4 will overcome current limitations by providing deep, wide-field HI imaging, allowing comprehensive investigation of how gravitational and hydrodynamical mechanisms operate across the full range of galaxy environments at resolved scales.

title: Magneto-rotational instabilities in solids: application to neutron-star crusts
comment: 13 pages, 4 figures. Accepted for publication in Phys. Rev. D
summary: The magneto-rotational instability can generate strong, turbulent substructure within magnetised shear flows. The efficacy of the mechanism as a function of microphysical aspects of the fluid, such as stratification and diffusivity, has been explored extensively. One aspect that has not been studied thus far, however, is whether the instability can also operate in solids. Motivated by the possibility that solid regions within planets or degenerate stars may rotate differentially with respect to liquid or gaseous layers during some phase of their life, we examine the extent to which elasticity suppresses the instability. A simplified, plane-parallel analysis reveals that only in cases where the flow is strongly sheared, such that the magnetic tension that would result from the instability in a liquid exceeds the shear modulus of the elastic cavity, can magnetic growth occur. In the context of dynamical tides in binary neutron-star mergers, this implies that the magnetic field can be amplified in the crust prior to coalescence only if the star boasts a spin frequency of $\gtrsim 300$Hz. If viscous heating weakens the crystalline structure prior to resonance, the required spin frequency is reduced.

AI.tldr: The paper investigates whether the magneto-rotational instability (MRI) can operate in solid elastic media (e.g., planetary or stellar crusts), finding that it requires strong shear such that magnetic tension exceeds the shear modulus, with implications for binary neutron-star mergers where amplification requires spin frequencies ≥300 Hz (or lower if viscous heating weakens the crystal).
AI.motivation: While MRI in magnetised shear flows has been extensively studied in fluids with stratification and diffusivity, its potential operation in solids has not been explored, despite the possibility that solid regions in planets or degenerate stars may rotate differentially relative to liquid/gaseous layers.
AI.method: A simplified, plane-parallel analytic analysis is performed to examine how elasticity suppresses MRI, comparing magnetic tension against the shear modulus of the elastic cavity.
AI.result: MRI operates in solids only when the shear is strong enough that magnetic tension exceeds the elastic shear modulus. For binary neutron-star mergers, crustal magnetic amplification requires a spin frequency ≥300 Hz, which can be lowered if viscous heating weakens the crystalline structure.
AI.conclusion: Elasticity suppresses MRI except under strongly sheared conditions. This sets a threshold for magnetic field amplification in solid astrophysical contexts such as neutron-star crusts prior to merger.

title: The VLA-COSMOS 3 GHz Large Project: Polarised source counts and catalogue
comment: 13 pages, 10 figures (main text). Accepted for publication in Astronomy and Astrophysics (A&A)
summary: The exploration of the faint polarised radio source population is essential for interpreting the nature and evolution of magnetic fields in galaxies. While recent studies have provided insight into source counts for the $μ$Jy polarised source population at 1.4 GHz, higher frequency surveys may be more sensitive to new populations that are depolarised at lower frequencies (i.e. due to internal or external depolarisation effects). We present the deepest polarised source counts at 3 GHz to date, at an angular resolution of $1.5''$. With these relatively higher frequency observations, we aim to probe the faint polarised star-forming galaxy (SFG) population. Furthermore, through spectral modelling, we aim to provide further insight into the frequency evolution of polarised source counts. We processed the polarisation data of the VLA-COSMOS 3 GHz Large Project, one of the deepest high-resolution radio continuum surveys. We produced Stokes Q and U mosaicked channel maps. After selecting known sources in total intensity, we performed 3D rotation measure synthesis and searched for polarised emission using an empirically determined threshold. With a sensitivity of 2.6 $μ$Jy/beam in Faraday depth, we detect 65 polarised sources (51 deg$^{-2}$) above our threshold. We find that our cumulative and Euclidean-normalised source counts at 3 GHz are consistent with those in the literature at 1.4 GHz, which we attribute to the combined effect of spectral index and depolarisation in the detected sources. We detect no SFGs in our sample and derive a 2$σ$ upper limit on the density of polarised SFGs of $<2.0~\mathrm{deg}^{-2}$. This implies that significantly deeper observations will be required to readily detect this population in the SKA-era.

AI.tldr: The paper presents the deepest polarised source counts at 3 GHz from VLA-COSMOS data, detecting 65 polarised sources (51 deg⁻²) with 2.6 μJy/beam sensitivity, finding consistency with 1.4 GHz counts due to spectral index and depolarisation effects, and reporting no detected polarised star-forming galaxies with a 2σ upper limit of <2.0 deg⁻².
AI.motivation: To explore the faint polarised radio source population at higher frequencies (3 GHz) to better probe populations that may be depolarised at lower frequencies, particularly star-forming galaxies, and to understand the frequency evolution of polarised source counts.
AI.method: Processed VLA-COSMOS 3 GHz Large Project polarisation data; produced Stokes Q and U mosaicked channel maps; performed 3D rotation measure synthesis on known total-intensity sources; used an empirically determined threshold to detect polarised emission.
AI.result: Detected 65 polarised sources (51 deg⁻²) at 2.6 μJy/beam sensitivity in Faraday depth; cumulative and Euclidean-normalised source counts at 3 GHz are consistent with 1.4 GHz literature; no SFGs detected; derived 2σ upper limit of <2.0 deg⁻² for polarised SFGs.
AI.conclusion: The consistency between 3 GHz and 1.4 GHz counts results from the combined effects of spectral index and depolarisation; significantly deeper observations are required to detect polarised star-forming galaxies in the SKA era.

title: Signatures of Two Distinct Epochs of FRB 20240114A from January to August 2024 Based on its Energy and Waiting Time Analysis
comment: 12 pages, 6 figures, accepted for publication in MNRAS
summary: A comprehensive analysis of the energy and waiting time distributions of the bursts from FRB 20240114A detected by the Five-hundred-meter Aperture Spherical Radio Telescope between 28 January and 29 August 2024 is presented. For the full sample, its energy distribution cannot be fitted with the simple power-law (SPL),bent power-law (BPL), thresholded power-law (TPL) or Band function models, and its waiting time distribution excluding intervals shorter than 0.5 s cannot be fitted with the Poisson or Weibull models. Nevertheless, for the subsamples with more than 50 bursts in single-day observations, their energy distributions can be fitted with the BPL or TPL models, and their waiting time distributions are better described by a Weibull model. It is noted that the best-fitting BPL parameter $β$ is approximately invariant within the epochs before and after 21 March 2024, with an average of $\bar β_b = 1.006 \pm 0.074$ and $\bar β_a = 1.236 \pm 0.183$ (one standard deviation), respectively. Most subsamples from the later epoch have a smaller burst rate parameter $r$ in the Weibull model than those from the earlier epoch. The majority of bursts with $E>10^{39}$ erg occurred in the earlier epoch. The energy distributions in the high-energy range ($> 6\times10^{37}$ erg) differ significantly between the two epochs, and power-law fits to $dN/dE$ yield indices of $-1.97_{-0.02}^{+0.02}$ and $-2.34_{-0.06}^{+0.06}$, respectively. The median of the waiting time distribution of the later epoch is larger than that in the earlier epoch. These results suggest that the two epochs may be dominated by different types of bursts, possibly attributed to changes in the physical properties of the emission region.

AI.tldr: Analysis of FRB 20240114A bursts detected by FAST (Jan–Aug 2024) shows that full-sample energy and waiting time distributions do not fit standard models, but single-day subsamples fit BPL/TPL and Weibull models. Two epochs (before/after March 21, 2024) exhibit distinct properties: different BPL β parameters, burst rates, high-energy distributions, and waiting time medians, suggesting different burst types due to changes in the emission region.
AI.motivation: To characterize the statistical properties (energy and waiting time distributions) of FRB 20240114A bursts detected by FAST and investigate possible epoch-dependent behavior.
AI.method: Fitting energy distributions with SPL, BPL, TPL, and Band function models; fitting waiting time distributions with Poisson and Weibull models; comparing subsamples from single-day observations and two epochs (before and after March 21, 2024).
AI.result: Full-sample energy and waiting time distributions do not fit standard models. Subsamples (>50 bursts/day) fit BPL/TPL energy and Weibull waiting time models. BPL β is ~1.006 (pre-March 21) vs ~1.236 (post-March 21). Later epoch has smaller burst rate r, larger waiting time median, and fewer high-energy (>10^39 erg) bursts. High-energy power-law indices differ: -1.97 (early) vs -2.34 (late).
AI.conclusion: The two epochs may be dominated by different burst types, likely reflecting changes in the physical properties of the emission region of FRB 20240114A.

title: Indicatives of Early Stages of Star Formation in the Universe
comment: 13 pages, 4 figures, published in Astrofizicheskii Byulleten
summary: The paper analyzes formation conditions for globular clusters (GCs) in circumgalactic clouds. The similarity between the metallicity distributions of GCs in the nearby Universe and of circumgalactic clouds is substantiated in detail over a wide range of redshifts: from \mbox{0.2} to \mbox{5.9}. The distributions of the number of circumgalactic clouds and GCs both contain a sequence of four local maxima at the metallicity values: \mbox{$[\rm{X/H}]\simeq -2.6, -2.0, -1.4,-0.5$}. The sequential enrichment of a circumgalactic cloud with a mass of $10^{8}\,M_{\odot}$ is calculated starting the extremely low metallicity \mbox{$ [\rm{X/H}] <-2.3$}, then following through the stages of \mbox{$-2.3 \le [\rm{X/H}]<-1.7$} and \mbox{$-1.7 \le [\rm{X/H}] < -0.9$} to the high metallicity \mbox{$[\rm{X/H}] \ge -0.9$}, where the boundaries of these ranges coincide with the local minima of the number of objects in the distributions. It is shown that for the reproduction of such distributions, it is sufficient that at each stage of enrichment of a part of a cloud in metals, one or more GCs with a total mass of \mbox{$3 \times 10^{6}\,M_{\odot}$} are formed. It is shown that the maximum mass of stars capable of leading to supernova explosions increases with the increase of metallicity. Possible values of this mass are calculated for the metallicities corresponding to the maxima in the distributions of clouds and GCs.

AI.tldr: The paper shows a strong correlation between the metallicity distributions of globular clusters (GCs) and circumgalactic clouds across redshifts 0.2–5.9, with both exhibiting four common peaks at [X/H] ≃ -2.6, -2.0, -1.4, -0.5. It models sequential enrichment of a 10⁸ M☉ circumgalactic cloud through four metallicity stages, finding that forming GCs with total mass ~3×10⁶ M☉ at each stage reproduces observed distributions. The maximum supernova-progenitor stellar mass is shown to increase with metallicity.
AI.motivation: To establish a causal link between globular cluster formation and the chemical enrichment history of circumgalactic clouds by comparing their metallicity distributions across a wide redshift range.
AI.method: Comparison of observed metallicity distributions of GCs and circumgalactic clouds from z=0.2 to 5.9; numerical modeling of sequential chemical enrichment of a 10⁸ M☉ cloud through four metallicity stages defined by distribution minima; calculation of maximum supernova-progenitor stellar mass as a function of metallicity.
AI.result: Both GCs and circumgalactic clouds share four identical local maxima in their metallicity distributions. A 10⁸ M☉ cloud enriched in four stages produces the observed distributions if 3×10⁶ M☉ of GCs form per stage. The upper mass limit for SN progenitors increases with metallicity.
AI.conclusion: GC formation is naturally explained by sequential metal enrichment in circumgalactic clouds, with the number of GCs and their metallicity tracing the cloud's enrichment history. Metallicity-dependent IMF or stellar evolution influences the maximum SN progenitor mass.

title: Bolometric correction factor and radiative efficiency for the super-Eddington accretion flow in tidal disruption events
comment: 9 pages, 5 figures, accepted for publication in MNRAS
summary: The estimate of the bolometric luminosity and the radiative efficiency are two key aspects for understanding the properties of the accretion flow around a supermassive black hole (BH). In this paper, we focus on the estimate of the bolometric luminosity and the radiative efficiency of the early super-Eddington accretion flow in tidal disruption events (TDEs). Specifically, we first perform radiation hydrodynamic simulations of super-Eddington accretion flow in TDE environment, and then calculate the corresponding emergent spectra with the method of post processing for the simulation data. Based on the emergent spectra, we calculate the isotropic-equivalent X-ray bolometric correction factor $k_\mathrm{bol}$ and the radiative efficiency $η$ of the super-Eddington accretion flow. We find that both $k_\mathrm{bol}$ and $η$ are BH mass and viewing-angle dependent. $k_\mathrm{bol}$ is in the range of about a few tens to a few thousands, and $η$ is in the range of $\sim 10^{-3}-10^{-1}$ for BH mass in the range of $10^{6-7}M_\odot$ and the viewing angle in the range of $0^{\rm o}-90^{\rm o}$. Finally, we apply the derived $k_\mathrm{bol}$ and $η$ to some specific TDEs to estimate the accreted mass during an event, which can significantly alleviate the so-called missing energy problem in TDEs.

AI.tldr: This paper uses radiation hydrodynamic simulations and post-processing spectral calculations to derive the X-ray bolometric correction factor (k_bol) and radiative efficiency (η) for super-Eddington accretion flows in tidal disruption events (TDEs), finding both are BH mass and viewing-angle dependent, with k_bol ranging from tens to thousands and η from ~10⁻³ to 10⁻¹, and applies these to real TDEs to alleviate the missing energy problem.
AI.motivation: To better understand the bolometric luminosity and radiative efficiency of super-Eddington accretion flows in TDEs, and to address the missing energy problem by providing improved estimates of accreted mass during such events.
AI.method: The authors perform radiation hydrodynamic simulations of super-Eddington accretion flows in TDE environments, followed by post-processing to calculate emergent spectra. From these spectra, they derive isotropic-equivalent X-ray bolometric correction factor k_bol and radiative efficiency η as functions of BH mass and viewing angle.
AI.result: k_bol ranges from a few tens to a few thousand; η ranges from ~10⁻³ to 10⁻¹ for BH masses 10⁶–10⁷ M⊙ and viewing angles 0°–90°. Both quantities are strongly dependent on BH mass and viewing angle.
AI.conclusion: Applying the derived k_bol and η to real TDEs yields improved estimates of accreted mass, significantly alleviating the missing energy problem.

title: Tracing grain growth in the forming prestellar core L1506C with 3D modeling of Herschel, IRAM, and CFHT observations
comment: 21 pages, accepted for publication in A&A
summary: In the early phases of star formation, properties of prestellar cores are commonly inferred from observations of thermal dust emission and thus depend on dust properties, which must be carefully characterized. Our target, L1506C, is part of the filament L1506 in the Taurus molecular cloud. The spectral energy distributions over the whole spectral range (from 160 μm to 2 mm), built from Herschel PACS and SPIRE and IRAM-NIKA2 data, have been fitted with a modified blackbody. These data were also modelled using the 3D radiative transfer code SOC and the latest THEMIS 2 dust model using extinction observations from WIRCam at CFHT and from Spitzer as additional constraints. The MBB modeling reveals that L1506C is fragmented into two low density cores with masses smaller than their Jeans masses. The dust color temperature and the emissivity spectral index show clear anti-correlation and change in grain properties. Grains more evolved than the diffuse interstellar medium are needed to model the densest part showing that grain growth already occurs at very early stage of star formation, even before the onset of gravitational collapse.

AI.tldr: L1506C in Taurus is fragmented into two sub-Jeans-mass cores. Dust modeling reveals grain growth (via THEMIS 2) before gravitational collapse, with an anti-correlation between dust temperature and emissivity spectral index.
AI.motivation: To characterize dust properties in prestellar cores, as dust emission models directly affect inferred core masses and evolutionary stage interpretations.
AI.method: SED fitting with modified blackbody (MBB) using Herschel PACS/SPIRE and IRAM-NIKA2 data; 3D radiative transfer modeling with SOC code and THEMIS 2 dust model, constrained by WIRCam/CFHT and Spitzer extinction observations.
AI.result: L1506C fragments into two low-density, Jeans-unstable cores; MBB shows anti-correlated dust color temperature and emissivity spectral index; THEMIS 2 modeling requires grains more evolved than diffuse ISM to fit densest regions.
AI.conclusion: Grain growth occurs at very early star formation stages, prior to gravitational collapse, indicating dust evolution begins in the prestellar phase.

title: X-ray Fourier lag-frequency spectra modulated by stochastic turbulent acceleration in the jets of high-frequency-peaked BL Lac
comment: 17 pages, 10 figures, published in PRD
summary: X-ray interband time lags are key diagnostics of jet physics and are frequently detected in high-frequency peaked BL Lac (HBL) objects at different epochs with various X-ray telescopes. In this work, we theoretically investigate Fourier lag-frequency spectra using a generic one-zone leptonic model incorporating the stochastic turbulent acceleration (STA), which plays a crucial role in shaping the emitted photon spectra. We demonstrate that the competition between STA, radiative cooling, and escape processes not only gives rise to two well-defined time-lag regimes: hard/positive and soft/negative lags, but also reveals the existence of a transition between the two regimes. Our results indicate that time lags in the transitional and soft-lag regimes can be clearly amplified and modified by STA's suppression of high-energy electron cooling, and nonlinear synchrotron self-Compton (SSC) cooling can further amplify the emergence of time lags. We conclude that the adopted model offers a unifying quantitative framework for interpreting the diverse time-lag signatures observed in the X-ray flares of HBLs. Additionally, SSC cooling effects can account for the relatively large lags observed in TeV-bright flares, as well as the observed trend between lag amplitude and flare duration: the larger the flare duration, the larger the lag.

AI.tldr: The paper investigates X-ray interband time lags in HBLs using a one-zone leptonic model with stochastic turbulent acceleration (STA), showing that the competition between STA, radiative cooling, and escape produces hard/positive lags, soft/negative lags, and a transition regime. SSC cooling amplifies time lags, explaining observed trends in TeV-bright flares and the correlation between lag amplitude and flare duration.
AI.motivation: To provide a unifying theoretical framework for interpreting diverse X-ray time-lag signatures observed in HBL objects across different epochs and telescopes, which are key diagnostics of jet physics.
AI.method: Theoretical analysis using a generic one-zone leptonic model that incorporates stochastic turbulent acceleration (STA), radiative cooling, and escape processes to compute Fourier lag-frequency spectra.
AI.result: Two well-defined time-lag regimes (hard/positive and soft/negative) plus a transition regime are identified. STA suppresses high-energy electron cooling, amplifying lags in transitional and soft-lag regimes. Nonlinear SSC cooling further amplifies lags and accounts for larger lags in TeV-bright flares and the positive correlation between lag amplitude and flare duration.
AI.conclusion: The adopted model provides a unifying quantitative framework for interpreting diverse time-lag signatures in HBL X-ray flares, with SSC cooling explaining the relatively large lags observed in TeV-bright flares and the lag-duration trend.

title: Assessing Ultra-Cool Dwarf Contamination in Photometrically Selected High-Redshift Galaxy Samples
summary: Ultra-cool dwarf stars (UCDs) are a common source of contamination in high-redshift galaxy searches as both sources are red and these early-forming galaxies can have sizes that are difficult to resolve even with space telescopes. Standard selection techniques, including photometric redshift estimation and color-color criteria, cannot fully eliminate this contamination. We develop \textbf{F}oreground \textbf{C}ontamination \textbf{E}valuator of \textbf{N}earby dwarf stars in high-\textbf{Z} photometrically selected \textbf{O}bjects (FC-ENZO), a code that predicts the number of dwarf stars misidentified as high-redshift galaxies for a given survey setup. FC-ENZO models the number of UCDs and evaluates the fraction of synthesized dwarf stars that passes user-specified selection methods. We compare two synthetic spectral energy distribution libraries and find that the ELF OWL library, which relaxes the assumption of chemical equilibrium, predicts larger contaminant fractions than the BOBCAT library, because of stronger absorption features around $ 1 $ \micron. The contamination fraction increases with metallicity and also depends on the adopted stellar number-density model. The dominant contaminants are T to early Y-type UCDs, which are most commonly misclassified as galaxies at $z \sim 8$. Comparing deep surveys from different space telescopes, we find similar overall contamination levels within the same redshift range. However, the contamination is concentrated near the limiting magnitude of each survey. At brighter magnitudes, the relative contamination is highest for HST (COSMOS), followed by Roman deep-tier survey, and JWST. Although the predicted contaminant numbers remain sensitive to model assumptions, FC-ENZO provides a practical tool for survey design and for identifying optimal fields for spectroscopic follow-up.

AI.tldr: FC-ENZO is a code that predicts contamination of ultra-cool dwarf stars (UCDs) misidentified as high-redshift galaxies in photometric surveys, finding that T to early Y-type UCDs are the main contaminants at z~8, with contamination levels depending on spectral libraries, metallicity, stellar density models, and survey sensitivity limits.
AI.motivation: Ultra-cool dwarf stars (UCDs) are a common source of contamination in high-redshift galaxy searches because both appear red and early-forming galaxies can have sizes hard to resolve even with space telescopes. Standard selection techniques like photometric redshift estimation and color-color criteria cannot fully eliminate this contamination.
AI.method: The authors develop FC-ENZO (Foreground Contamination Evaluator of Nearby dwarf stars in high-Z photometrically selected Objects), which models UCD numbers and evaluates the fraction of synthesized dwarf stars that pass user-specified selection methods. They compare two synthetic spectral energy distribution libraries (ELF OWL and BOBCAT) and test different stellar number-density models.
AI.result: The ELF OWL library (relaxing chemical equilibrium assumption) predicts larger contaminant fractions than BOBCAT due to stronger absorption features around 1 µm. Contamination increases with metallicity and depends on the stellar number-density model. Dominant contaminants are T to early Y-type UCDs misclassified as galaxies at z~8. Similar overall contamination levels across deep surveys (HST COSMOS, Roman, JWST), but concentrated near each survey's limiting magnitude.
AI.conclusion: Although predicted contaminant numbers remain sensitive to model assumptions, FC-ENZO provides a practical tool for survey design and identifying optimal fields for spectroscopic follow-up to mitigate UCD contamination.

title: Polarization Architecture of Steady GRMHD Jets from the Horizon to Infinity
comment: 22 pages, 8 figures
summary: We develop a semi-analytic framework for stationary, axisymmetric GRMHD jets that efficiently generates resolved polarized images from the near-horizon region out to $\sim 10^5\,r_g$ across a broad parameter space, enabling rapid exploration of how gravity and magnetohydrodynamic flows imprint scale-dependent signatures on jet morphology and polarization. We identify a new scale-dependent separation in polarimetric diagnostics. Outside the photon ring, plasma loading strongly modifies the polarization-angle profile of the integrated jet-layer emission through inertia-driven winding of the magnetic field. At large image-plane radii, the polarization angle follows a power-law in radius, with an index determined by the jet collimation profile. Near the horizon, in contrast, jets converge to a universal polarization pattern controlled solely by black hole spin. This convergence is hierarchical: differences in velocity and magnetic-field structure are erased first, whereas collimation-dependent differences persist to smaller radii, thereby allowing these effects to be disentangled. These results establish a largely achromatic polarimetric diagnostic that connects GRMHD jet dynamics to resolved image structure, with direct implications for high-resolution polarimetry and for constraining black hole spin and jet formation.

AI.tldr: The paper develops a semi-analytic framework for GRMHD jets to rapidly generate resolved polarized images across a wide parameter space, identifying scale-dependent polarimetric signatures: universal polarization near the horizon controlled by black hole spin, and power-law polarization-angle profiles at large radii set by jet collimation, enabling new diagnostics for black hole spin and jet formation.
AI.motivation: To enable rapid exploration of how gravity and magnetohydrodynamic flows imprint scale-dependent signatures on jet morphology and polarization across a broad parameter space, from the near-horizon region to ~10^5 r_g.
AI.method: A semi-analytic framework for stationary, axisymmetric GRMHD jets that efficiently generates resolved polarized images.
AI.result: Identified a scale-dependent separation in polarimetric diagnostics: (1) outside the photon ring, plasma loading modifies polarization angle via inertia-driven magnetic field winding; (2) at large radii, polarization angle follows a power-law in radius with index determined by jet collimation; (3) near the horizon, jets converge to a universal polarization pattern controlled solely by black hole spin, with hierarchical erasure of velocity/magnetic-field differences before collimation differences.
AI.conclusion: Establishes a largely achromatic polarimetric diagnostic connecting GRMHD jet dynamics to resolved image structure, with direct implications for high-resolution polarimetry and for constraining black hole spin and jet formation.

title: The Road to Identifying the Earliest Radio-Powerful AGN with the SKA
comment: Published in Advancing Astrophysics with the SKA II (AASKAII), 2026 (arXiv:2606.20366). Report-no:AASKAII/Afonso01. Advancing Astrophysics with the SKA II (AASKAII) outlines the transformative scientific advances that will be enabled by the SKA telescopes
summary:
The Epoch of Reionization (EoR) is one of the most pivotal frontiers in modern astrophysics, marking the emergence of the first galaxies, stars, and supermassive black holes (SMBHs). Despite insights from the Atacama Large Millimetre/submillimetre Array and the James Webb Space Telescope, we still struggle to explain how $\sim10^{9}$ M$_\odot$ SMBHs powering luminous active galactic nuclei (AGN) already exist by $z\sim7$. The recent discovery of powerful radio emission from some of these early AGN is notable, offering new constraints on early black-hole accretion and, with the Square Kilometre Array Observatory (SKAO), the prospect of directly probing neutral hydrogen through 21-cm absorption studies.
  Yet progress remains slow: only a few radio-powerful AGN are known at $z>6$, far fewer than theoretical predictions suggest, raising questions about whether this reflects intrinsic properties or selection biases and incomplete spectral information.
  In this chapter we synthesise predictions from state-of-the-art hydrodynamical and semi-analytic simulations with observational constraints from SKAO pathfinder facilities. These models suggest the existence of a substantial, still-undetected population of radio-powerful AGN in the EoR, but show that present surveys are limited by selection biases and incomplete radio spectral information.
  We discuss a physically motivated strategy for identifying high-redshift radio AGN, based on broadband radio spectral energy distributions, spectral curvature, dynamical jet evolution, and radio-only redshift estimation, offering a transformative alternative to traditional empirical approaches.
  Finally, we justify how the sensitivity and spectral coverage of the SKAO will allow fine-frequency sampling across the 50 MHz - 15 GHz range, revolutionising our ability to identify the earliest radio-powerful AGN and probe the earliest SMBHs.

AI.tldr: This chapter reviews the challenge of explaining supermassive black holes (~10⁹ M☉) powering luminous AGN at z~7, synthesizes predictions from simulations with SKAO pathfinder observations, identifies a substantial undetected population of radio-powerful AGN limited by selection biases, proposes a physically motivated identification strategy using broadband radio SEDs and spectral curvature, and forecasts how SKAO's sensitivity and spectral coverage will transform detection of early radio-powerful AGN and 21-cm absorption studies of neutral hydrogen.
AI.motivation: To address the tension between theoretical predictions and the sparse observational detection of radio-powerful AGN at z>6, which hinders understanding of early SMBH formation and accretion.
AI.method: Synthesis of state-of-the-art hydrodynamical and semi-analytic simulations with observational constraints from SKAO pathfinder facilities; physically motivated strategy based on broadband radio SEDs, spectral curvature, dynamical jet evolution, and radio-only redshift estimation.
AI.result: Models predict a substantial undetected population of radio-powerful AGN in the EoR; current surveys are limited by selection biases and incomplete radio spectral information.
AI.conclusion: SKAO's fine-frequency sampling across 50 MHz–15 GHz will revolutionize the identification of the earliest radio-powerful AGN and enable direct 21-cm absorption studies of neutral hydrogen, transforming our ability to probe early SMBH growth.

title: Colour evolution in the radio afterglow of GRB 241025A
comment: Accepted for publication in A&A
summary: We present the observing campaign of the afterglow of GRB241025A, a gamma-ray burst (GRB) whose prompt emission has been simultaneously detected by Swift, Einstein Probe, Fermi/GBM, SVOM, Konus-Wind and VZLUSAT-2 3U CubeSat. Our multi-wavelength campaign comprises radio, near-infrared, Optical and X-ray observations. The afterglow was clearly detected in all bands. We performed a semi-empirical fit of the data, showing that the afterglow behaviour can be reasonably reproduced by a single component, i.e. an ultra-relativistic shock. However, the results from the semi-empirical fit are inconsistent with the predicted evolution from the standard afterglow model in the slow cooling regime. Specifically, we found that at early times the synchrotron self-absorption frequency $ν_a$ should be at higher frequencies with respect to the ones sampled by our campaign, in order to explain the observed colour evolution in radio, namely the spectral evolution in time. To reconcile the prediction from the standard model with the observed data set, we fit the observations with a semi-analytical model, including a multiplicative factor $τ_{enh}$ to the optical depth which, in turn, artificially increases $ν_a$. We found that the radio colour evolution, together with the near-infrared, optical and X-ray emission, can be described reasonably well by a forward shock from a structured jet, provided that the optical depth in the shocked material is enhanced by a factor $τ_{enh}=500$. We suggest that such enhancement in the optical depth can result from a population of cold electrons in the downstream material, i.e. electrons that were not accelerated by Fermi I process at the shock front, in agreement with the theoretical expectations previously reported in the literature. Overall, our work underscores the importance of systematic, multi-frequency, multi-epoch radio follow-ups of these extreme events.

AI.tldr: The paper presents multi-wavelength observations of GRB241025A afterglow (radio to X-ray). The emission is consistent with a single ultra-relativistic shock, but the standard model fails to explain the radio colour evolution. A structured jet forward shock model with enhanced optical depth (τ_enh=500) fits the data, possibly due to cold electrons in the downstream not accelerated by Fermi I process.
AI.motivation: To understand the afterglow emission mechanism of GRB241025A, a gamma-ray burst detected by multiple observatories (Swift, Einstein Probe, Fermi/GBM, SVOM, Konus-Wind, VZLUSAT-2), and to reconcile discrepancies between standard afterglow model predictions and observed multi-wavelength data.
AI.method: Multi-wavelength observing campaign (radio, NIR, optical, X-ray); semi-empirical fitting; semi-analytical modeling with a structured jet forward shock and an enhanced optical depth factor τ_enh.
AI.result: The semi-empirical fit showed a single ultra-relativistic shock reproduces the afterglow, but is inconsistent with the standard slow-cooling model. The radio colour evolution requires the synchrotron self-absorption frequency ν_a to be higher than observed. A structured jet forward shock model with τ_enh=500 successfully describes all bands.
AI.conclusion: The enhanced optical depth is attributed to cold electrons in the downstream not accelerated by Fermi I process, consistent with theoretical expectations. The work highlights the importance of systematic, multi-frequency, multi-epoch radio follow-ups of GRBs.

title: The Merger-Driven Origin of the Vast Extended Stellar Disc Around the Andromeda Galaxy
comment: 16 pages (13 + 3 Appendix), 15 figures, abstract abridged for arXiv, submitted to A&A, comments welcomed
summary: The closest giant spiral, the Andromeda galaxy (M31), shows compelling evidence for a recent, gas-rich major merger event.
